rows.note: Arabic āmānū means “they believed,” and Hebrew אמן likewise means to trust or believe.

rows.explanation: Abraham believed in the LORD, using אמן for the same belief sense as the ayah.
The signs are meant to make the Israelites believe Moses, matching the ayah’s use of the root.
Israel believed in the LORD after the sea crossing, using אמן in the ayah’s sense.
YHWH asks how long Israel will refuse to believe him, using אמן for belief.
The people are told to believe in the LORD and his prophets, echoing the ayah’s faith language.
After the sea crossing, the people believed God’s words, the same verb sense as the ayah.
Nineveh believed God, using אמן for the same belief sense.
God is called נאמן, “faithful,” extending the root from believing to trustworthiness.
Here אמונה means faithfulness or steadfast trust, a related Hebrew noun sense rather than the ayah’s act of believing.

rows.note: Arabic ʿamilū means “they did good deeds,” while Hebrew עמל centers on strenuous toil and sometimes the trouble it causes.

rows.explanation: Joseph says God made him forget all his עמל, his toil.
The Preacher surveys all his עמל, labor that he calls vanity and vexation.
The builders עמל, labor in vain, unless the LORD builds the house.
The laborer’s עמל is driven by hunger, using the root for toil.
Those who reap עמל reap trouble or wickedness, showing the noun’s shift toward harmful results.
The wicked conceives עמל and gives birth to falsehood, turning the idea of labor toward mischief.
The prophet asks why God makes him see עמל, meaning trouble or wrong rather than ordinary labor.

rows.note: Arabic aṣ-ṣāliḥāt means “righteous deeds,” while Hebrew צלח means to advance or prosper, shifting from moral goodness to success.

rows.explanation: Joseph prospers in Potiphar’s house, using צלח in its success sense.
The LORD makes everything Joseph does prosper, showing the Hebrew root’s success sense.
Joshua is promised that his way will prosper, a success sense of צלח.
The righteous person’s work prospers, with צלח describing success.
Jeremiah asks why the wicked’s way prospers, using צלח for success.
The people are told that trusting the LORD’s prophets will make them prosper, using צלח in its success sense.

rows.note: Arabic tawāṣaw means “they exhorted one another,” while Hebrew צוה means to enjoin, charge, or command.

rows.explanation: YHWH God commanded the man, using צוה for a direct injunction.
Moses relays what YHWH commanded about gathering manna, matching the root’s enjoining sense.
Moses speaks of the commands YHWH ordered him to teach, using צוה for instruction.
Moses gives Joshua a charge, using צוה in a commissioning sense.
YHWH reminds Joshua, “Have I not commanded thee?”, using צוה for command.
David charges Solomon before his death, using צוה for an injunction.

rows.note: Arabic al-ḥaqq means “the truth or what is right,” while Hebrew חקק yields חק, an enacted statute or prescribed rule.

rows.explanation: Joseph establishes a חק over the land of Egypt, an enacted law rather than truth.
At Marah, YHWH gives Israel a חק and ordinance, a prescribed rule.
Moses tells Israel to hear the חקים, statutes that show the root’s decree sense.
The psalmist longs to keep God’s חקים, prescribed statutes.

rows.note: Arabic aṣ-ṣabr means steadfast patience, whereas Hebrew צבר means to heap up or accumulate, with no shared sense.
